section: Controlled Drainage Effects on Flow and Losses
subsection: Nitrate and Phosphorus Loss Reductions and the Flow--Load Coupling
note:
The paper says reduced nitrate loss in a moderately well-drained soil was mainly due to reduced tile effluent rather than increased denitrification. The checked claim assigns this caution to poorly drained soils, which is not what the cited text supports.
"Gilliam et al. (1979) evaluated whether CD [controlled drainage] could reduce nitrate loss from fields... They found that in a moderately well-drained soil, a large reduction in N03-N loss occurred because of the reduced tile effluent, and not because of increased denitrification."
paragraph: Denitrification provides a secondary but well-documented loss-reduction mechanism where the water table is held high. Canadian farm-scale work found a greater relative abundance of nitrate-reducing/facultative bacteria under controlled drainage, supporting denitrification as a nitrate-loss pathway, while also reducing total suspended solids and particulate phosphorus by damping macropore flow \parencite{Tanga2025}. However, several syntheses caution that in poorly drained soils the nitrate reduction is attributable mainly to reduced tile effluent rather than to increased denitrification **[CITATION CHECKED: THOMAS1995]**, and Albanian field data found nutrient concentrations were not strongly affected by drainage-system type, with outflow volume the dominant control on total nutrient transport \parencite{Grazhdani1996}. Modeling in Belgium reproduced an adverse relationship between denitrification and leaching---wider spacings and higher water tables increase denitrification and reduce leaching but also reduce plant uptake---so that total winter NO$_3$-N losses could be substantially reduced under controlled drainage \parencite{ElSadek2002,ElSadek2002b}.

section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: Salt leaching, drainage-water reuse, and disposal
note: The paper studies subsurface drain spacing/depth effects on sugarcane yield under waterlogging in Venezuela; it never discusses soil salinity or salinization anywhere in the text. Its only economic statement concerns whether drainage investment is justified for yield protection, not for salinization prevention.
paragraph: Removing salt from soil relocates the problem to the drainage water, whose management is among the most persistent challenges. Environmentally acceptable disposal methods are needed \parencite{Ayars2014,Steppuhn2006}, evaporation-pond management must be tested at full scale and combined with volume/contamination reduction \parencite{BRADFORD1991}, and trace-element fate---arsenic speciation and uranium recovery or removal---compounds the problem \parencite{Gao2007,Duff1997,Gao2003}. Emerging treatment routes are at the demonstration stage: electrolysis of saline wastewater at varying salinity \parencite{Yang2023}, sorptive filter materials tested with real rather than artificial drainage water \parencite{Pugliese2023}, and blending of drainage and reverse-osmosis product water \parencite{Singh2020d}. Reuse-focused research spans site-specific load--flow relationships, germination-stage salinity tolerance, and improved scheduling that meets crop evapotranspiration from a shallow water table while minimising upward salt flow \parencite{WESTCOT1988}, provisional field guidance on substituting drainage water for wheat \parencite{Sharma1998}, blending and evaporation-pond storage \parencite{Datta2002}, farm-level reuse within a basin-wide salt balance \parencite{Qureshi2008}, seasonal groundwater undulation and drip conversion to prevent accumulation \parencite{Mirlas2021,Dou2022,Singh2019}, and biochar, phytoremediation, and reclamation innovations \parencite{Liu2025f,Steppuhn2017,Youngs2000}. Comprehensive assessment of waterlogging and salinity together, rather than separately, is recommended \parencite{Valipour2014}, and the economic feasibility of drainage as a preventive measure against salinisation remains to be established **[CITATION CHECKED: HalbacCotoaraZamfir2022]**.

subsection: Design Levers: Spacing, Depth, Outlet Control, and Enhanced Configurations
note: The paper is a Great Lakes and Cornbelt water-quality review. It reports nitrate-load reductions and general water-table-management benefits, but it does not support Dutch yield increases, 170-410 mm infiltration, or a 64 percent yield gain.
paragraph: Shallow, multi-level, and enhanced configurations extend these principles. Shallow drainage reproduces much of the flow- and load-reduction benefit, reducing Iowa subsurface volume by 46--58\% and nitrate by 29--49\% generally without reducing yield \parencite{Helmers2012,Schott2017}; a multi-state analysis found quicker water-table drawdown, reduced yield variability, and 3.4~cm less total flow than deep drains, though with more surface runoff and a lower benefit--cost ratio \parencite{Ghane2021b}. In saline irrigated settings drain depth controls exported salinity: Australian deep drains flowed continuously and exported the largest salt loads (5867~kg~ha$^{-1}$) whereas shallow drains flowed only after irrigation, with low salinity and the greatest salt-load reduction \parencite{Christen2001b}. Multi-level (bilevel) systems cut the time the water table exceeded 0.5, 0.75, and 1.0~m by 84\%, 67\%, and 41\% and produced much lower shallow-drain salinity (4.7 versus 31.7~dS~m$^{-1}$) while removing similar total salt \parencite{Hornbuckle2007}; analytical theory shows adding shallow drains between deep drains raises drainage rate and allows wider deep-drain spacing \parencite{Hornbuckle2012}, and managed deep drains occupy an intermediate position \parencite{Ayars2006b,Christen2001b}. Engineered enhancements alter flow further: a permeable filter increased discharge (about 1.9 times conventional) and accelerated drawdown while reducing runoff \parencite{Tao2016,Tao2017}; combined open-ditch-plus-subsurface designs improved waterlogging removal \parencite{Ren2021,Tao2025}; siphon-type drainage raised flow rates 27--90\% \parencite{Ren2023}; artificial macropore tubes generated flow where none occurred and desalinated the profile \parencite{Chen2021}; and supplementary drainage of a clay field raised mean annual discharge 2.6-fold and cut topsoil runoff by 75\% \parencite{Häggblom2019}. Controlled drainage with subirrigation raised groundwater levels, supplied 170--410~mm of infiltration, and increased Dutch yields by up to 64\% **[CITATION CHECKED: FAUSEY1995]**, while land retirement with drains closed can eliminate drainage entirely \parencite{Purkey2001}.

section: Salinity, Reclamation, and Drainage-Water Reuse in Arid and Irrigated Systems
subsection: Salt-leaching dynamics and long-term reclamation trajectories
note: "A long-term study regarding nutrient loss and water pollution due to surface and subsurface drainage in heavy-textured coastal saline soil is necessary."
paragraph: The recurring message is temporal: meaningful salt reduction often accrues so slowly that short observation windows systematically underestimate long-term benefit, and only extended drainage with sustained monitoring resolves the true trajectory \parencite{Almen2021,Daigh2025}. The long-term effects of combined saline-water irrigation and subsurface drainage on both salinity and yield require further evaluation \parencite{Feng2017,Feng2021}, desalination rates and trends remain incompletely quantified \parencite{Guo2024b,Yao2024}, and controlled drainage introduces unresolved temporal trade-offs, buffering outflow while risking salt accumulation **[CITATION CHECKED: Islam2025]**. Longer observation records paired with optimal leaching quotas and cost--benefit analysis are needed to close these gaps \parencite{Guo2025}, and salt-tolerant crops in reclamation rotations, alongside quantification of rainfall and irrigation-efficiency gains relative to salt-removal capacity, remain to be characterised \parencite{Qadir2001,Castanheira2010}.

section: Drainage Hydrology: Flow Pathways, Regime, and Scaling
subsection: Tile Drainage as a Dominant Flow Pathway
note:
The content mostly comes from another citation (also being cited at the same location).
“Watershed scale analysis derived the tile drainage contribution to stream flow (QT/Q) from a numerical tracer driven analysis of instream surface water. During precipitation events tile drainage represented 30% of stream flow, whereas during intervals between precipitations events, 61% of stream flow originated from the tile system...Regression for all of the NOPs, produced a slight increasing trend with increasing DA (slope = 0.12), from QT/Q of 0.29 at 6 km2 to 0.39 at 45 km2.”
paragraph: Partitioning between tile and surface pathways varies systematically with hydrologic condition and drainage area. In Iowa, tile drainage averaged 30\% of streamflow during events but 61\% during non-event periods; the event ratio $Q_T/Q$ rose with drainage area while the non-event ratio fell, and annual $Q_T/Q$ increased log-linearly from 0.29 at 6~km$^2$ to 0.39 at 45~km$^2$ ($R^2=0.98$) **[CITATION CHECKED: King2014]**.

section: Nitrate Export: Magnitudes and Biophysical Controls
note: Mainly from another refs at the same locations, "Results from the model indicated that drainageway soils with a denitrification rate of 0.015 day−1 would reduce upland nitrate concentrations below 0.5 mg L−1 at the catchment outlet."
paragraph: Dual-isotope studies indicate that drainage nitrate is often derived largely from organic sources (manure and soil organic matter) via nitrification, with denitrification not always dominant. In Ontario, $\delta^{15}$N and $\delta^{18}$O relationships lacked the 2:1 denitrification slope, pointing to organic sources and continued nitrification through all seasons \parencite{Smith2011,Smith2011b}, and rapid nitrification of applied ammonium ($>90\%$ within $72$~h) supplies ready nitrate for leaching \parencite{Hu2024}. Where denitrification is active it is detectable: along Polish flow paths nitrate declined while sulfate, excess N$_2$, $\delta^{15}$N, and $\delta^{18}$O increased \parencite{Dragon2016}, and nested French watersheds implied $34$--$82\%$ nitrate retention dominated by underground denitrification \parencite{Billy2011,Billy2013}. In Iowa drainageways, denitrification in slowly permeable soils could remove essentially all upland groundwater nitrate, functioning as a natural treatment system **[CITATION CHECKED: Cambardella1999]**. Yet where drains intercept water before it reaches these attenuating zones, export is high: tile discharge is dominated by pre-event water---three-component separation gave $65\%$ groundwater and $29\%$ shallow soil water---yet tile drains carried the highest NO$_3$-N of any source and contributed over $99\%$ of watershed nitrate export \parencite{Williams2022,Grose2022}.

section: Agronomic Benefits: Yield, Salinity Reclamation, and Socio-Economics
subsection: Salt leaching and reclamation of saline and waterlogged soils
note: This paper focus on testing the hydraulic conductivity and clogging of geotextile, which is highly related to the discussed points. The cited numerics comes from another paper. "The salt removal rate of the geotextile-wrapped subsurface pipes was more than 95%. The salt removal rate of the double-layer geotextile scenario was the highest (96.7%),"
paragraph: Closer spacing and greater depth shorten the desalinization period and increase salt removal, though depth benefits saturate. A DRAINMOD analysis found salinity fell $55.5\%$ in two years at $20$~m spacing but only $5.9\%$ in five years at $200$~m, a slightly-saline target within a decade requiring spacing below $30$~m \parencite{Chen2025}; the meta-analysis generalises this into climate-specific layouts (spacing $>30$~m and depth $>1.2$~m in humid climates; $10$--$20$~m spacing in arid climates with shallow water tables) \parencite{Yang2025}. Field and column studies identify optima near $15$--$20$~m \parencite{Wang2020,Han2023,Chen2022}, with desalination decaying beyond about $30$~m \parencite{Zhu2025b}. Depth effects are pronounced but bounded---pipes shallower than $1.0$~m are essentially invalid for discharging salt \parencite{Qian2021b}, yet returns diminish beyond about $1.4$~m \parencite{Bahçeci2007,Bahçeci2006}, and an intermediate $0.8$--$1.2$~m depth is often preferred under saline irrigation, saving $10$--$15\%$ water \parencite{Feng2017,Muhammad2021}. Envelope and filter design is a first-order control: the envelope factor dominates pipe material, a double-layer geotextile achieving $>95\%$ salt removal while triple layers clog **[CITATION CHECKED: Elzoghby2021]**. Economic analyses converge on roughly $20$~m spacing at $1.2$~m depth as the maximum-return layout \parencite{Chen2025}.

section: Modeling, Measurement, and Mapping of Drainage Systems
note:
The paper is about using ML method to predict tile draiange area, however the reported details are from other referred papers.
"he point-based assessment for the testing dataset indicates that the classification model achieved good overall accuracy, with a score of 0.96, thus 96 % of tile and non-tile points, are classified correctly. Recall and precision are 0.96 and 0.85, respectively. The balanced accuracy and F1 scores are 0.96 and 0.90, respectively. These metrics demonstrate the good quality of the classification model."
paragraph: Data-driven methods frequently match or outperform process models for the specific outputs on which they are trained while requiring less data and computation. Neural networks predicted real-time water-table control and saturated conductivity more accurately than pedotransfer functions (the ANN prediction of saturated conductivity reaching $R^2$ up to 0.96), random forests outperformed linear regression for agronomic prediction, and an Attention~U-Net surrogate reached test $R^2$ of 0.997--1 for head, drainage volume, and salt discharge while drastically reducing computation \parencite{Yang2000,Ellafi2021,Djiemon2019,Lei2026,Sarangi2006,Bakhsh2005b,Bakhsh2007b}. Parsimonious surrogates (Cubist, SVM, NIT-DRAIN) can match process models for flow while training far faster, though process models remain preferable for climate extrapolation \parencite{Sharma2003,Negm2016,Frederiksen2023,Chelil2022,Li2025}. Remote sensing combined with deep learning now maps drained extent at regional to national scales with accuracies commonly exceeding 85--96\% and totals within a few percent of census estimates: AgTile-US reported 22.34~Mha ($-0.35\%$ versus USDA) and SEETileDrain achieved 0.96 testing accuracy **[CITATION CHECKED: Moller2018]**, while convolutional segmentation networks reliably delineate visible drain lines and outperform classical edge detectors \parencite{Redoloza2023,Song2021,Woo2023,Naz2009}. Ancillary sensing infers drainage-relevant surface conditions through SAR, Landsat SWIR, and vegetation indices \parencite{Meunier2001,Rijal2013,Xu2018,Khanal2020}. Finally, kriging-family methods are consistently the most reliable interpolators for the spatially variable soil properties governing drain spacing: in the Nile Delta, conductivity was isotropic with a 5.6~km range and kriged values were recommended as design inputs, while accounting for variability widened spacing about 5\% and saved substantial pipe, and neglecting $K_{sat}$ variability could bias design spacing by $-27\%$ to $+3\%$ \parencite{GALLICHAND1991,GALLICHAND1992,GALLICHAND1993,Moustafa1998b,Moustafa2000,Moustafa1998,Akis2015,Sepaskhah2004}.
